title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 361
paragraphs: Of these two accounts, every man may adopt the one he finds more credible when he hears it. I, for my part, have already stated my own opinion about them. For if these too, like Heracles son of Amphitryon, had appeared before all men's eyes and lived their lives into old age in Hellas — I mean Dionysos son of Semele and Pan son of Penelope — then one might have said that these also had been born as mere men, bearing the names of gods who had come into being long before. But as it is, with regard to Dionysos the Greeks say that as soon as he was born, Zeus sewed him up in his thigh and carried him to Nysa, which is above Egypt in the land of Ethiopia; and as for Pan, they cannot say where he went after he was born. From this it has become clear to me that the Greeks learned the names of these gods later than those of the other gods, and they trace their lineage as though their birth occurred at the time they first learned their names.
So far, then, the history is told by the Egyptians themselves;
